Error pattern: Success comes from separating state-dependent properties from amount-dependent ones.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does changing container, sample size, or energy input make this property change while the material stays the same?
Use when: Relevant on matter-property questions comparing solid vs liquid or small vs large samples.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt asks about a specific sample’s current shape, exact quantity, or changing conditions over time.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what orbits the atom’s center, then select the negatively charged particle outside the central core.
Error pattern: Success came from recalling the basic atomic structure: a central nucleus with surrounding electrons.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map each candidate to location and role: central core, core constituents, or surrounding particle; choose only the surrounding one.
Use when: Apply this to introductory science items about atom parts, locations, charges, or simple structural relationships.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt concerns modern orbital probability clouds, subatomic interactions, or non-classical models beyond basic classroom structure.

Transfer rule: If asked which structure occurs in every organism, then choose the smallest universal unit shared by both single-celled and multicellular life.
Error pattern: Success came from checking biological universality across all life forms, not assuming complexity-based structures are always present.
Diagnostic check: Test each candidate against a one-celled organism; eliminate anything that cannot exist in a single cell.
Use when: Apply this on biology questions about traits, structures, or organization levels claimed to be present in all organisms.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question limits the group to multicellular organisms, specific kingdoms, or developmental stages.

Transfer rule: If two equal time intervals cover different distances, then the interval with more distance had the higher average speed.
Error pattern: Success comes from mapping average speed to distance-per-equal-time, not inventing causes like terrain, direction, or constancy.
Diagnostic check: Verify the time spans are the same length; then compare distances only and infer which interval’s average speed was greater.
Use when: Apply to motion questions that compare travel over equal durations and ask what must be true about speed.
Boundary: Ignore when the intervals differ in length or the question asks about route details, acceleration, or causes not determined by distance-time data.

Transfer rule: If a science question asks why repeated trials help, then choose the effect on reliability/error reduction, not on proving a hypothesis.
Error pattern: Mistook replication as confirmation of a claim instead of a method for reducing random error and improving accuracy.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this option mention better evidence quality or merely stronger proof?” Reject choices centered on proof alone.
Use when: Apply to experimental-design items about repetition, sample size, averaging, reliability, accuracy, or sources of error.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is about statistical significance, causation, or whether results support a specific theory independent of measurement error.

Transfer rule: If asked how to make an electromagnet stronger, then compare changes by whether they increase current, coil turns, or magnetic core quality.
Error pattern: Success came from using the causal factors of electromagnet strength instead of surface features of the device.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, sort each option into increases current, decreases current, increases turns, decreases turns, improves core, or weakens core; choose the strengthening category.
Use when: Apply this on questions about simple electromagnets, solenoids, relays, bells, or magnetic field strength from circuits.
Boundary: Ignore this when the magnet is permanent, the question targets resistance alone, or another design constraint overrides raw field strength.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for total mass after combining substances, then add the masses of all components unless a loss is stated.
Error pattern: I treated dissolving as making one part “disappear,” ignoring conservation of mass in mixtures.
Diagnostic check: List each starting mass, sum them, and ask: “Is any material removed, spilled, evaporated, or reacted into something excluded?”
Use when: Apply this to word problems about mixing, dissolving, combining ingredients, or forming a solution with given masses.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the problem gives volume instead of mass, specifies mass loss/gain, or uses non-additive measurements.

Transfer rule: If heat moves through direct physical contact within a material or between touching objects, then classify it as conduction.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing contact-based transfer from transfer across space or via moving fluid.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would the warming still happen without touching and without bulk air/liquid motion?” If no, conduction is likely.
Use when: Apply this on heat-transfer questions contrasting solids, touching objects, air circulation, flames, sunlight, or distance effects.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the main mechanism is fluid flow, electromagnetic emission, or when multiple mechanisms are equally central.

Transfer rule: If both parents show a recessive trait, then assign each a homozygous recessive genotype and predict all offspring recessive.
Error pattern: Confusing phenotype ratios from mixed-dominance crosses with the guaranteed outcome of two recessive-phenotype parents.
Diagnostic check: Write the parent genotypes from the stated phenotypes, make a 2×2 Punnett setup, and verify whether any dominant allele can appear.
Use when: A genetics question gives dominance information and asks for offspring from parents whose phenotypes are explicitly stated.
Boundary: Ignore this when inheritance is non-Mendelian, phenotype does not map directly to genotype, or linkage/epistasis is involved.

Transfer rule: If a question asks the function of an animal body covering, then choose the option describing its primary survival role, not an incidental appearance effect.
Error pattern: Success came from prioritizing core biological function over decorative, signaling, or unrelated processes.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would the structure still be useful if no one saw it?” If yes, favor defense or physiology over display.
Use when: Relevant for anatomy-to-function multiple-choice items about coverings, shells, skin features, feathers, fur, or similar external structures.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt explicitly asks about secondary functions, mating signals, camouflage, or species-specific exceptions.

Transfer rule: If a question asks how to describe an object’s position or motion relative to somewhere, then identify the reference point or frame first.
Error pattern: Success came from using the definition of position correctly instead of choosing extra motion details that are not always required.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Could I state where the object is without naming what it is compared to?” If not, choose the comparison baseline.
Use when: Apply this to items about location, displacement, motion description, or how position changes over time.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task specifically asks for speed, acceleration, rate, or path details rather than relative location.

Transfer rule: If choices mix stored-energy forms with motion/wave/heat forms, then pick the one based on energy stored in matter or position.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying by mechanism, not by examples that merely “seem energetic.”
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Is the energy present because something is stored and could be released later, or because particles/waves are currently moving?”
Use when: Relevant in questions asking to sort energy types into potential versus kinetic categories.
Boundary: Ignore when the task uses specialized physics definitions, combined forms, or asks about energy transformations rather than category labels.

Transfer rule: If a question asks how a juvenile animal avoids predators, then prefer a trait that directly reduces detection or capture before advanced movement develops.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the trait to survival function rather than to unrelated life stage, feeding, or communication details.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it immediately lower predation risk in the stated stage, and can I name the mechanism in one phrase?
Use when: Apply this to biology items about adaptations, camouflage, juvenile vulnerability, or function of body patterns versus other traits.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about reproduction, diet, parental care, or a trait’s role after the vulnerable stage.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what most directly supports reaching a conclusion, then choose the step that analyzes collected evidence rather than setup, alternatives, or forecasts.
Error pattern: Success came from prioritizing evidence-to-claim reasoning over preparatory or speculative steps.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Which option would let me justify a conclusion from observations right now?” Eliminate any option that only organizes, generates possibilities, or predicts.
Use when: Apply this to investigation or scientific-method questions asking for the key step in drawing conclusions from results.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about planning, hypothesis formation, procedure design, or prediction before data exist.

Transfer rule: If a biology term includes “selectively permeable,” then choose the statement about controlling what enters and leaves, not total blocking or unrelated roles.
Error pattern: Success comes from matching the term to its core function; failures confuse regulation with absolute exclusion, mere structure, or a specific substance.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each choice: does it describe both entry and exit control for some materials but not all materials?
Use when: Apply this on life-science questions about membrane function, transport, homeostasis, or definitions of permeability-related vocabulary.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about a different organelle, a special transport mechanism, or structural support rather than membrane selectivity.

Transfer rule: If a question links a species’ sound use to added environmental noise, then choose the effect that directly disrupts communication/navigation behavior.  
Error pattern: Success came from tracing the nearest causal pathway instead of jumping to broad ecosystem, genetic, or physical changes.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state the organism’s named function, add the disturbance, and ask which option most immediately blocks that function.  
Use when: Apply this for biology items about sensory signals, communication, navigation, mating calls, echolocation, or habitat noise/light interference.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt gives evidence of toxin exposure, food-web changes, mutation mechanisms, or another stronger non-sensory cause.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what determines an organism’s species/body plan from a fertilized egg, then choose inherited genetic information over traits like age, size, or sex.
Error pattern: Success came from distinguishing foundational developmental causes from incidental characteristics.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option by asking, “Would changing only this factor reliably change the kind of organism that develops?”
Use when: Apply this to basic biology items about development, heredity, embryos, species identity, or what directs growth from fertilization.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about later development, health, sex-specific traits, or environmental effects within the same organism type.

Transfer rule: If a downstream product inhibits an earlier step in its own production chain, then classify the loop as negative feedback.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the direction of influence in the pathway rather than matching surface vocabulary.
Diagnostic check: Draw arrows for each conversion, then add the product’s effect on the earlier step; if the effect is inhibitory, mark it negative.
Use when: Relevant in pathway, regulation, homeostasis, or control questions where an output acts back on an upstream stage.
Boundary: Ignore when no backward influence is stated, or when the effect amplifies rather than suppresses the earlier step.

Transfer rule: If a cosmology question asks what the Big Bang theory says, then choose the option describing an early extremely dense, hot origin with later expansion.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the core model statement, not drifting to unrelated steady-state, cyclic, or current-process claims.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, reject choices that describe what the universe is doing now or deny an initial high-density state.
Use when: Apply this to multiple-choice items about standard Big Bang basics, universe origin models, or contrasts with alternative cosmologies.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for evidence, timelines, inflation details, element formation, or the fate of the universe.

Transfer rule: If asked for the primary energy source driving evaporation from open water, then choose the external radiative input heating the surface.
Error pattern: Success came from identifying the underlying driver rather than nearby processes, transports, or secondary contributors.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Which option adds most energy directly to surface molecules so they can escape into vapor?”
Use when: Apply for water-cycle, phase-change, or Earth-system questions asking for the main cause of evaporation or surface heating.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks about local modifiers, biological water release, subsurface heating, or motion effects rather than the primary energy source.

Transfer rule: If a question asks why a material covers or surrounds an electrical part, then check whether the material’s key property is insulating rather than conducting.
Error pattern: Success came from linking a material’s function in a device to its physical property, not to effects like speed or circuit completion.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this material stop charge from passing through it?” If yes, prefer the insulation-based choice.
Use when: Apply this on basic electricity items about coatings, handles, casings, or safety around current-carrying parts.
Boundary: Ignore this when the material is used specifically to connect components, carry current, or alter resistance by design.

Transfer rule: If asked for evidence of evolution, then compare inherited traits across organisms from different times or generations, not changes within one individual.
Error pattern: Success came from separating evolutionary change in populations over time from development, healing, or sex-based variation within a species.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this comparison involve two organisms from different historical periods whose skeleton differences could reflect inherited change?”
Use when: Apply for questions contrasting evolution with growth, injury recovery, reproduction, or other within-lifetime changes in anatomy.
Boundary: Ignore when the task is about individual development, healing, sexual dimorphism, or short-term physiological change rather than lineage change.

Transfer rule: If choices mix metals with a noble gas, then pick the noble gas as least electrically conductive under standard conditions.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: classify each option by bonding/state first instead of comparing familiar metals directly.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label every option metal, nonmetal, or noble gas, then ask which lacks mobile electrons in its normal state.
Use when: Relevant for multiple-choice questions on conductivity, especially when elemental identity matters more than detailed numeric properties.
Boundary: Ignore when the problem specifies plasma, ionized gas, dissolved species, extreme conditions, or unusual forms like graphite or molten materials.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what process creates loose sediment that makes up a beach surface, then choose the process that physically breaks rock into smaller pieces.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the landform’s visible material to the direct geologic process instead of broader or less direct Earth processes.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Does this process directly produce sand/pebbles by physical breakup at the surface, rather than moving material, altering minerals, or creating new rock?”
Use when: Apply this to landforms described by their surface material, especially where choices mix weathering, transport, chemistry, and internal Earth processes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about transport, deposition, underground formation, or mineral composition change.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for a product of a biological process, then recall the process’s inputs and outputs before choosing.
Error pattern: Success came from using a process model instead of matching familiar words from the topic.
Diagnostic check: Write a quick input→process→output chain and verify the option is produced, not merely required or enabling.
Use when: Apply this to science questions about cycles, reactions, or systems with named substances, energies, and products.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about structure, location, definition, or a fact not based on process outputs.

Transfer rule: If objects share the same speed and stopping conditions, then rank required stopping force by mass; greater mass needs greater force.
Error pattern: Success came from applying proportional reasoning between mass and force under matched motion conditions.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, verify speed is equal, compare masses only, and ask whether any stopping time or distance is specified.
Use when: Relevant in mechanics questions comparing how hard it is to stop, accelerate, or change motion for different masses.
Boundary: Ignore this when speeds differ, stopping time/distance changes, or other forces and collision details control the outcome.

Transfer rule: If a question asks which body system is analogous to intracellular chemical signaling from surface to control center, then choose the system based on long-distance messenger communication.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the underlying signaling mechanism, not superficial anatomy or location.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state the source, messenger, travel path, and target; select the option that preserves all four roles most closely.
Use when: Apply this on analogy questions comparing cell communication processes with organ-system functions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question focuses on waste removal, barrier protection, fluid return, or non-signaling structural roles.

Transfer rule: If asked which organism is least involved in decay, then choose the one not functioning primarily as a decomposer or detritivore.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying roles by ecological function instead of grouping all living things near dead matter together.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask: does it directly break down dead tissue or feed on detritus as a normal role?
Use when: Apply on ecology questions contrasting decomposers, scavengers, consumers, and ordinary living structures associated with soil or dead material.
Boundary: Ignore when the item asks about indirect nutrient cycling, soil stabilization, or cases where non-decomposers influence decay without doing the breakdown.

Transfer rule: If a question asks which plant part performs a function, then match the organ to its main biological role before choosing.
Error pattern: Confused intake or storage functions with the primary job of the named structure instead of recalling standard organ-function pairs.
Diagnostic check: List the part’s key task in one phrase, then reject any option describing a function mainly done by a different plant organ.
Use when: Relevant for biology items about specialized structures in multicellular organisms, especially plant organs and their distinct functions.
Boundary: Ignore when the question concerns atypical adaptations, engineered plants, or asks about a secondary rather than primary function.

Transfer rule: If a body signal appears during activity, then match it to the immediate need that signal is designed to prompt.
Error pattern: Success came from linking a symptom to its direct homeostatic purpose rather than to a generic comfort or performance action.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What specific deficit or risk does this signal indicate right now, and which choice directly corrects it?”
Use when: Apply this on biology or health questions about exercise, body cues, regulation, or basic survival responses.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about long-term training strategy, safety protocol, or a response caused mainly by social context.

Transfer rule: If a fuel source comes from farming a crop, then check for environmental costs of intensified agriculture before supply effects.
Error pattern: I overfocused on the feedstock becoming scarce and ignored resource depletion caused by repeated cultivation.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does increased demand mainly change output quantity, or does it more directly strain soil, water, or land quality?” Choose the direct consequence.
Use when: A question links biofuels, crop-based products, or expanded farming to possible negative impacts.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is about short-term market pricing, processing technology, or non-agricultural energy sources.

Transfer rule: If a question asks why something cooks, warms, or changes temperature, then choose the option describing heat transfer to a cooler target.
Error pattern: Confusing a helpful physical trait like movement or access with the actual causal mechanism that produces the outcome.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this option directly explain energy flowing into the food, or only describe how the medium reaches it?”
Use when: Apply for science items about heating, cooking, warming, cooling, or phase-related effects where several properties seem relevant.
Boundary: Ignore when the question explicitly asks about transport, coverage, penetration, or mechanical action rather than temperature change.

Transfer rule: If a question asks how to make findings more reliable, then choose the action that adds repeated trials while keeping conditions unchanged.
Error pattern: Reliability questions reward replication and consistency, not changing variables or removing the comparison being tested.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each option as repeat, control, or change; prefer repeat unless the prompt asks about fairness or validity instead.
Use when: Apply this on experiment-design items about improving confidence, consistency, or trustworthiness of measured results.
Boundary: Ignore this when the issue is an uncontrolled variable, biased measurement, or an unfair comparison rather than reliability.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what occupies most atomic volume, then choose the diffuse particle cloud, not the dense central core.
Error pattern: I confused where most mass is concentrated with where most space is occupied.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, separately identify which component holds nearly all mass and which extends farthest from the center; they are often different.
Use when: This applies to basic structure questions contrasting central subatomic parts with surrounding ones, especially mass-versus-volume distinctions.
Boundary: Ignore this when asked about mass, charge, particle count, or size of a specific subatomic particle rather than overall atomic volume.

Transfer rule: If a question asks which graph fits data changing across time, then choose the graph that connects ordered points to show trends.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the graph type to its core purpose instead of being distracted by other display features.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Is time on one axis, and do I need to see increase, decrease, or rate of change across observations?”
Use when: Apply this for chart-selection items involving trends, sequences, repeated measurements, or relationships tracked over intervals.
Boundary: Ignore this when the goal is comparing categories, showing part-to-whole composition, or using icons rather than plotted values.

Transfer rule: If a biology question asks for the plant process most like vertebrate sexual reproduction, then choose the one involving fusion of gametes from two different parents.
Error pattern: I matched a later developmental outcome instead of the reproductive event that creates genetic mixing between parents.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this step transfer male gametes to female structures from another individual and enable fertilization?”
Use when: Apply this for analogy questions comparing plant life-cycle steps with animal sexual reproduction, especially among pollination, growth, division, and development terms.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about asexual reproduction, mitosis-only processes, or post-fertilization development rather than mate-to-mate gamete exchange.

Transfer rule: If nutrients trigger algal blooms that cut light and lower dissolved oxygen, then predict declines in oxygen-dependent aquatic animals.  
Error pattern: Success came from tracing the full causal chain through indirect ecosystem effects rather than stopping at the first change.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, write the sequence nutrient rise → algae rise → light down/oxygen down, then ask which choice matches a downstream consequence of low oxygen.  
Use when: Apply this on ecology questions describing food webs, eutrophication, trophic cascades, or multi-step environmental cause-and-effect.  
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about immediate chemical changes only, or gives evidence that species thrive in low-oxygen conditions.

Transfer rule: If asked about a giant planet’s rings, then recall they are primarily solid icy material mixed with rocky dust, not atmospheric gases.
Error pattern: Success came from using domain knowledge about ring composition instead of matching options to the planet’s atmospheric makeup.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Is this option a ring material or a planet-atmosphere component?” Eliminate gas-dominated choices first.
Use when: Apply this on astronomy questions about ring systems, especially when choices mix gases, molecules, debris terms, and solid materials.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question concerns a planet’s atmosphere, moons, formation history, or a ring system unlike the major outer-planet rings.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what energy form directly produces light, then choose the form that is light itself, not a byproduct source or side effect.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the physical phenomenon to its direct energy category rather than a related process.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Is this option the emitted light wave, or merely motion, stored energy, or waste heating?”
Use when: Apply this to energy-conversion questions about bulbs, glowing objects, radiation, or devices described as producing visible light.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks for total energy output, primary input, efficiency losses, or all forms produced.

Transfer rule: If a device reduces hydrocarbon and nitrogen-oxide emissions, then infer it lowers formation of secondary air pollution rather than changing unrelated gases.
Error pattern: Success came from linking removed exhaust precursors to their downstream environmental effect.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the named pollutants, recall what they chemically produce in air, and reject choices about substances not targeted by the device.
Use when: Apply this to pollution-control questions that mention specific emitted chemicals and ask about broader atmospheric outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about engine efficiency, greenhouse warming, or direct emissions not affected by precursor removal.

Transfer rule: If a process describes blood flowing through an organ while wastes/extra water are removed, then pair the blood-transport system with the waste-excretion organ system.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping each verb to a system’s core job instead of choosing by nearby body terms alone.
Diagnostic check: Underline transport medium, material removed, and organ named; confirm one system moves blood and the other produces/stores/excretes liquid waste.
Use when: Relevant in physiology questions linking kidney function, blood flow, filtration, excretion, or interactions between body systems.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about gas exchange, food breakdown/absorption, or organs not handling blood filtration and urine production.

Transfer rule: If one parent is homozygous dominant and the other is homozygous recessive for a simple dominant/recessive trait, then all first-generation offspring are heterozygous and show the dominant phenotype.
Error pattern: I treated a parental cross like a mixed-allele cross, failing to derive offspring genotypes before estimating phenotypes.
Diagnostic check: Write each parent’s two alleles, combine one from each into all offspring boxes, and confirm whether every box has the same genotype.
Use when: Apply this to single-gene inheritance questions with complete dominance and explicitly stated homozygous parental genotypes.
Boundary: Ignore this when dominance is incomplete/codominant, multiple genes are involved, or offspring are from later generations or test crosses.

Transfer rule: If asked what enables or prevents weather, then check first whether a substantial atmosphere exists.  
Error pattern: Success came from linking weather to the medium that carries winds, clouds, and pressure-driven changes.  
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Can gases here circulate enough to transport heat, moisture, or particles and form changing conditions?”  
Use when: Apply to questions about planets, moons, or surfaces comparing weather, climate, erosion, or day-to-day environmental change.  
Boundary: Ignore when the question is specifically about geology, internal heat, magnetism, or composition unrelated to atmospheric processes.

Transfer rule: If a question asks how to change a material into a specific state, then choose the action that moves temperature in the direction needed for that state change.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: matching the target state with the physical condition that causes it, instead of picking an unrelated action.
Diagnostic check: Name the starting state and target state, then ask, “Does this option reliably cool, heat, compress, or otherwise cause that exact transition?”
Use when: Apply this on basic science items about states of matter, temperature effects, and everyday material changes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the change depends mainly on chemistry, pressure, or mixing rather than simple temperature change.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for distance between stars, then choose the large-scale astronomy unit based on light travel over time, not everyday or local-orbit units.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the measurement scale to the context instead of defaulting to familiar Earth-based units.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compare the unit’s typical range: terrestrial, within a planetary system, or interstellar; select the one explicitly used for interstellar spans.
Use when: Apply this for astronomy questions involving extremely large separations between celestial objects beyond a single solar system.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question concerns local travel, planet-to-sun distances, or brightness/time rather than distance.

Transfer rule: If one parent is homozygous dominant, then no offspring can show the recessive phenotype, regardless of the other parent’s hidden recessive allele.
Error pattern: I focused on the heterozygous parent’s recessive allele and ignored that the other parent always blocks a recessive pair.
Diagnostic check: Write the gametes from each parent and test whether any offspring genotype can be homozygous recessive; if none, eliminate any nonzero recessive-phenotype percentage.
Use when: Apply this to single-gene dominance questions about offspring probabilities, especially when one parent is pure dominant and the question asks for recessive outcomes.
Boundary: Ignore this when inheritance is not simple dominant-recessive, such as linkage, multiple genes, incomplete dominance, or penetrance effects.

Transfer rule: If a question asks which Earth-layer trait enables plate movement, then choose the trait describing mechanical flow or plasticity, not unrelated electromagnetic or energy effects.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the mechanism to the observed process instead of picking a true-but-irrelevant property.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, state “What directly lets rigid plates move?” and verify the option names a deformable, slowly flowing state.
Use when: Apply this on Earth science items linking an interior layer’s characteristics to tectonics, convection, or surface-motion evidence.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about composition, radiation interactions, heat storage alone, or magnetic recording rather than motion mechanics.

Transfer rule: If particle kinetic energy increases in a phase-change question, then choose the change toward a less ordered, higher-energy state.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping energy increase to greater molecular motion and weaker intermolecular binding, not to cooling or condensation.
Diagnostic check: Rank phases by molecular freedom—solid < liquid < gas; verify the option moves upward on that scale when energy rises.
Use when: Apply this to matter-state or heating/cooling items involving particles, temperature, evaporation, melting, freezing, condensation, or sublimation.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question concerns chemical reactions, pressure-driven effects without heating, or exceptions dominated by unusual phase diagrams.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what most affects a young animal’s physical trait, then check whether the trait is primarily inherited before considering environment or behavior.
Error pattern: Successful pattern: distinguishing innate biological traits from external influences that may alter condition but not baseline appearance.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would this trait usually be set by genes at birth, or changed mainly by surroundings after birth?”
Use when: Apply to biology items comparing heredity with habitat, food, training, or actions as causes of visible characteristics.
Boundary: Ignore when the trait is explicitly learned, temporary, injury-related, age-dependent, or known to change directly from environment.

Transfer rule: If choices mix common materials, then classify each by free-charge mobility and favor the one with metallic bonding.
Error pattern: Success came from using material properties instead of surface-level familiarity or everyday usage associations.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, sort options into conductor, semiconductor, or insulator; verify only one has many mobile electrons at room conditions.
Use when: Apply this on basic physical-property questions comparing everyday substances for electrical conduction or similar transport behavior.
Boundary: Ignore this when conditions change conduction strongly, such as solutions, temperature extremes, impurities, or composites with coatings.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what must occur before a valid scientific conclusion, then choose the step that directly establishes support through evidence collection, not later communication steps.
Error pattern: Distinguishing core epistemic requirements from optional or subsequent dissemination activities.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Could the conclusion be justified even if no one else was informed yet?” If yes, eliminate communication, publication, and discussion choices.
Use when: Relevant for science-process items contrasting evidence-gathering with sharing, reporting, or peer interaction.
Boundary: Ignore when the question asks about improving credibility, replication, peer review, ethics, or what happens after evidence is already obtained.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for a particle model of a state of matter, then match the choice to particle spacing and freedom of motion, not surface theme.
Error pattern: Success came from using the core microscopic property: particles in this state stay closely packed in fixed positions and only vibrate.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: are the “particles” packed closely and mostly staying in place rather than traveling around?
Use when: Apply this to analogy or representation questions about solids, liquids, and gases, especially when choices describe people, objects, or vehicles moving differently.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the problem depends on chemical identity, bonding type, temperature changes, or changes of state rather than particle arrangement.

Transfer rule: If one factor is changed between otherwise identical groups, then choose that manipulated factor as the variable being tested.
Error pattern: Success came from isolating the independent variable instead of focusing on controlled conditions or repeated setup details.
Diagnostic check: List all conditions, mark what is kept constant, then verify the only systematic difference across groups before answering.
Use when: Experimental descriptions compare groups, mention controls, and ask what variable’s effect is being studied.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about outcomes, constants, confounders, or when multiple factors change together.

Transfer rule: If a question links seafloor ridges with a measured widening rate, then choose the process driven by plate motion at a divergent boundary.
Error pattern: Success came from matching observed ocean-basin growth to the underlying geologic mechanism rather than a surface-level effect.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: does the option create new crust and explain both ridge formation and basin spreading over time?
Use when: Apply this on Earth science items about ocean floors, mid-ocean ridges, seafloor spreading, crust formation, or long-term basin expansion.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the scenario is about short-term shoreline change, sediment buildup, or non-tectonic surface processes only.

Transfer rule: If a plant-structure question asks how water moves through the plant, then choose the option describing internal transport vessels, not energy-making or pigments.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the organ’s function to its physical transport mechanism rather than confusing transport with photosynthesis or food production.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Does this choice describe moving water/materials through pathways, or does it describe making energy, color, or food?”
Use when: Apply this on elementary biology items about plant parts, especially stems, roots, leaves, and movement of water or nutrients.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about light capture, gas exchange, reproduction, or chemical products instead of transport.

Transfer rule: If a claim rests on one limited experiment, then require independent repetition or multiple trials before treating the result as publishable.
Error pattern: Reliability questions are solved by checking reproducibility, not by changing variables unrelated to verification.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would repeating the same method several times directly test whether the finding is stable?” If yes, favor that action.
Use when: The prompt mentions limited samples, surprising findings, publication decisions, or later failure to reproduce results.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question is about hypothesis generation, ethical limits, or intentionally testing a different condition rather than confirming robustness.

Transfer rule: If a trait change is a recurring seasonal body-state change, then classify it as a physical adaptation, not behavior, learning, or mutation.
Error pattern: Success came from separating inherited/physiological traits from actions and from one-time DNA changes.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Is the organism doing something, acquiring something through experience, or expressing a built-in bodily trait on a cycle?
Use when: Apply to questions contrasting mutation, learned behavior, behavioral adaptation, and physical adaptation for seasonal or life-stage trait changes.
Boundary: Ignore when the prompt is about a novel DNA change, a voluntary action, or a skill gained through practice or experience.

Transfer rule: If a plant trait changes leaf size in a layered ecosystem, then link it to the limiting resource at that layer, especially light near the ground.
Error pattern: Success came from matching a structural feature to an environmental constraint rather than choosing a generic survival need.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, identify the organism’s position in the habitat, ask what resource is reduced there, and verify the trait would improve capture of that resource.
Use when: Apply this to ecology items about adaptations, niches, canopy/shade effects, or traits of organisms living beneath others.
Boundary: Ignore this when the trait is explained by reproduction, defense, temperature control, or a directly stated non-resource cause.

Transfer rule: If asked why something is a mixture, then choose the statement about parts remaining physically combined while each keeps its own properties.
Error pattern: Used an overly broad definition that fits many multi-substance cases but does not distinguish mixtures from compounds or other classifications.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option by asking: does it uniquely separate mixtures from chemically combined substances and allow physical separation?
Use when: Relevant for classification questions about foods, materials, or samples made from visible or named components combined without reaction.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the question asks only for composition count, solution type, phase, or evidence of a chemical change.

Transfer rule: If a joint is straightening, then identify the agonist as the muscle that produces extension and the antagonist as the opposing flexor that relaxes.
Error pattern: Mixed up opposing muscles by choosing the one used for curling instead of matching muscle action to the requested movement.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mime the motion and ask: “Is this flexion or extension, and which named muscle is the extensor at this joint?”
Use when: Apply for anatomy or movement questions about antagonistic muscle pairs acting across a hinge joint during bending versus straightening.
Boundary: Ignore when the movement is at a different joint type, involves stabilization only, or asks about force, injury, or simultaneous co-contraction.

Transfer rule: If choices mix inherited traits with injuries or temporary/body-maintained conditions, then select the trait determined by genes at birth.
Error pattern: Success came from separating heritable genetic characteristics from acquired changes caused by environment, accidents, or grooming.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Can this be passed through DNA from parent to child without any life event after birth?”
Use when: Apply on biology questions about inheritance, traits, offspring, genes, or parent-to-child transmission.
Boundary: Ignore when the question concerns learned behaviors, contagious conditions, prenatal damage, or traits strongly altered by later choices or events.

Transfer rule: If asked for the most common element in a normal main-sequence star, then choose the element that dominates stellar composition and fusion fuel.
Error pattern: Success came from recalling a core astronomy fact instead of overthinking less abundant but familiar elements.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “What element makes up most of ordinary stars by mass and is the starting fuel for stellar fusion?”
Use when: This applies to basic astronomy questions about stellar composition, especially ordinary stars like the Sun.
Boundary: Ignore this for questions about planets, stellar remnants, trace spectral lines, or unusually evolved stars with altered surface composition.

Transfer rule: If a trait is said to evolve because it helps attract mates or improve mating success, then choose the outcome involving greater reproductive success, not mere survival.
Error pattern: Success came from linking evolution to differential reproduction rather than to habitat, predation alone, or unrelated interactions.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Which option directly increases the number of offspring carrying the trait?” Eliminate choices that only describe conditions, risks, or cross-species behavior.
Use when: Apply this on natural-selection questions about display traits, camouflage during breeding, courtship signals, or seasonal reproductive changes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about immediate function, ecological mechanism, or proximate cause rather than why selection favored the trait.

Transfer rule: If asked for a learned behavior, then choose an action the animal does, not a built-in body trait or passive sense.
Error pattern: Confused anatomical adaptations and sensory capacities with behavior acquired or used through experience.
Diagnostic check: For each choice, ask “Is this a body feature, a general ability, or an observable act?” Eliminate features/abilities; keep deliberate acts.
Use when: Relevant in biology questions contrasting learned behavior with structural adaptations, inherited traits, or sensory characteristics.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the prompt asks about physical adaptations, innate traits, or when all options are behaviors rather than mixed types.

Transfer rule: If a health factor is a routine, voluntary behavior under personal control, then classify it as a lifestyle-related factor.
Error pattern: Success came from separating modifiable daily habits from external conditions, inherited traits, and clinician-directed actions.
Diagnostic check: Ask: Is this usually chosen day to day by most adults, and can it change without changing genes, surroundings, or a prescription?
Use when: Apply this on health-classification items contrasting behavior-based factors with environmental, genetic, or treatment-based categories.
Boundary: Ignore this when the behavior is explicitly mandated by a clinician or strongly constrained by circumstance rather than ordinary choice.

Transfer rule: If an animal trait changes with seasonal background color, then infer its main function is camouflage with the surroundings.
Error pattern: Success came from linking a changing visible trait to survival advantage by matching environment-dependent appearance, not unrelated functions.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does the trait track external conditions like season or habitat, and does that improve concealment more directly than temperature or activity?”
Use when: A question describes color, pattern, or appearance shifts across seasons, habitats, or life stages and asks what the change enables.
Boundary: Ignore this when the trait is explicitly tied to waterproofing, insulation, signaling, mating, or a non-visibility function.

Transfer rule: If asked how microbes benefit the body, then check for a direct, well-known biological function they perform inside the body, especially digestion.
Error pattern: Success came from matching a beneficial organism to its established physiological role instead of choosing a major body function handled by other systems.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Do microbes directly do this in normal human biology, or is it mainly done by bones, blood, lungs, or temperature-control systems?”
Use when: Apply this on life-science questions about helpful bacteria, symbiosis, microbiome functions, or human body processes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about harmful microbes, nonhuman organisms, or indirect effects not involving a normal body function.

Transfer rule: If a safety rule restricts clothing or footwear before a lab, then link it to the specific body-part injury the item would expose, not to preventing the hazard itself.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the rule to protective equipment logic: exposure reduction over comfort, convenience, or unlikely secondary effects.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What body area is uncovered, and what common lab accidents could directly harm it?” Choose the rationale that names that injury prevention.
Use when: A question asks why a teacher, lab, or workplace requires certain attire or bans exposed skin during hands-on science activities.
Boundary: Ignore this when the rule is clearly about contamination control, electrical design, or task performance rather than personal protective coverage.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what animals do during immediate weather changes, then choose a short-term behavioral response over seasonal or bodily changes.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the time scale of the cause with the time scale of the response.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label each option as immediate behavior, long-term adaptation, seasonal cycle, or physical change; keep only options matching the trigger’s duration.
Use when: Apply this to biology or everyday-life multiple-choice items about responses to sudden environmental conditions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about long-term climate, life-cycle patterns, or evolutionary traits.

Transfer rule: If an environmental stressor alters soil chemistry or damages leaves/needles, then choose the broad outcome of reduced long-term plant health rather than an absolute or beneficial effect.
Error pattern: Success came from linking mechanism to ecosystem-level trend and rejecting extreme wording.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, test each option for causality and scope: does it match known effects, avoid “all/always,” and describe the most likely net result over time?
Use when: Apply this to ecology questions about pollutants, deposition, nutrient loss, or plant/forest responses.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks for a short-term, species-specific, or directly measured chemical change instead of overall biological impact.

Transfer rule: If one sedimentary layer has fossils and an adjacent one does not, then first test whether depositional conditions changed between layers.
Error pattern: Success came from comparing layer-forming environments instead of forcing a local destructive process after deposition.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Would this choice mainly alter what lived or was buried here, rather than simply reshape, remove, or concentrate material later?”
Use when: The question contrasts fossil presence versus absence across sedimentary layers, especially with limited evidence besides the layers themselves.
Boundary: Ignore this when clues indicate metamorphism, direct fossil destruction, missing rock from nondeposition/erosion, or fossils were never expected to preserve.

Transfer rule: If asked which elements have the most similar properties, then first compare group/column placement; choose elements in the same vertical group, not just nearby or both “reactive.”
Error pattern: Confusing broad periodic-table categories or invented shared traits instead of using the strongest predictor of similarity: valence-electron pattern from group membership.
Diagnostic check: For each candidate pair, write each element’s group and typical valence-electron count; prefer the pair with matching group and similar common ion/bonding behavior.
Use when: This applies to periodic-table questions about “similar properties,” reactivity trends, bonding tendencies, or likely ion formation.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question targets exceptions, isotopes, allotropes, or nonperiodic factors like specific compounds or conditions.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what best sets a population’s size in a habitat, then choose the key limiting resource that directly affects survival and reproduction.
Error pattern: Success came from using ecological carrying-capacity reasoning instead of surface habitat features or unrelated species counts.
Diagnostic check: List each choice and ask, “Does this directly limit births, deaths, or sustained energy intake?” Eliminate choices with only indirect or weak effects.
Use when: Apply this on ecosystem, population, habitat, or carrying-capacity questions comparing abiotic conditions, vegetation, other organisms, and resources.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt asks about a short-term trigger, a species-specific dependency, or a factor explicitly stated as dominant in the scenario.

Transfer rule: If two objects at different temperatures touch, then infer heat transfers from the hotter object to the colder one by conduction.
Error pattern: Success came from applying the temperature-gradient rule instead of tracking substance movement or vague “flow” wording.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, label which object is hotter, which is colder, and verify the chosen mechanism is direct contact heat transfer.
Use when: Relevant for everyday thermal situations involving touching solids, melting, warming, or cooling with no fluid motion emphasized.
Boundary: Ignore when the question centers on fluids, bulk motion, electromagnetic transfer across a gap, or phase-change details beyond heat direction.

Transfer rule: If choices vary in temporal scale, then prefer the long-term abiotic factor that directly controls primary growth and survival over short-term or indirect influences.
Error pattern: Success came from comparing drivers by magnitude, duration, and directness rather than choosing visible but minor biological activity.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does it directly alter plant productivity or community composition across many seasons, and is its effect larger than daily or localized effects?
Use when: This applies to ecosystem-change questions asking what causes the greatest change over time among weather, time-scale, and organism-count factors.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question targets immediate conditions, a specific species interaction, or short-term behavior rather than long-term habitat change.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for a conclusion from a table, then compare the relevant totals directly before choosing a summary statement.
Error pattern: Chose a broad claim without verifying it against the table’s counts; likely reversed or skimmed category totals.
Diagnostic check: List each category, sum or read its total, and ask, “Which total is larger?” before selecting any conclusion.
Use when: Relevant for data tables, charts, or graphs asking which group is greater, more common, or more numerous.
Boundary: Ignore when the task depends on causes, behaviors, or relationships not measured by the displayed quantities.

Transfer rule: If asked which activity conserves water, then choose the option that reduces water demand or avoids unnecessary use over time.
Error pattern: Success came from selecting the practice with built-in efficiency rather than one involving continued or redundant water use.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: does this action lower total water needed, or does it spend extra water without necessity?
Use when: Apply this on everyday conservation questions comparing habits, landscaping, cleaning, or agriculture choices.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about another resource, or when reducing water use creates a separate stated harm that changes the goal.

Transfer rule: If body movement is produced by muscles, then trace the source to stored fuel in the body and map it to motion/work, not ambient warming.
Error pattern: Confused a byproduct of a process with the input source, choosing what accompanies movement instead of what powers it.
Diagnostic check: Identify the immediate energy store before motion starts; ask “What reserve is being consumed to contract muscle fibers?” and verify the output is movement.
Use when: The scenario involves organisms, muscles, exercise, trembling, or any internal process causing limbs or joints to move.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question explicitly states an external heater, friction, falling objects, batteries, or changing height/stretch instead of metabolism.

Transfer rule: If several examples are given, then test each answer choice against every example and keep only the shared property.
Error pattern: Success came from intersecting attributes across items instead of focusing on a feature true for only one or two.
Diagnostic check: For each option, make a quick table with the examples and mark yes/no; reject any option with even one no.
Use when: This applies to classification questions asking what different objects have in common or share as a category.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task asks for a difference, an exception, a process, or a context-dependent property.

Transfer rule: If an example shows an organism eating, drinking, or absorbing food, then classify it as obtaining nutrients rather than another life process.
Error pattern: Success comes from mapping the observed action to the direct biological function instead of nearby but different body processes.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “What is the organism actively doing right now?” If the action is getting material for energy or growth, choose nutrient intake.
Use when: Apply this to basic life-process questions with verbs about feeding, swallowing, consuming, or absorbing.
Boundary: Ignore this when the example centers on gas exchange, offspring production, movement alone, or removal of wastes after digestion.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what multiple populations living in the same place form, then choose the term for an assemblage of populations, not an environment or a single lineage.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the biological level of organization correctly and separating group terms from place terms.
Diagnostic check: Replace the target word with “many kinds living together here”; if it still fits, prefer the collective-organism term.
Use when: This applies to ecology vocabulary questions contrasting organism groupings, locations, and taxonomic units.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt is about one population only, abiotic surroundings, or evolutionary classification.

Transfer rule: If an enzyme’s activity changes after moving to a new body region, then compare environmental conditions there—especially pH—to the enzyme’s operating range.
Error pattern: Success came from matching enzyme function to denaturation/inactivation by chemical environment rather than to amount of substrate or physical mixing.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the changed variables after the transition and ask which one directly alters enzyme shape or active-site function.
Use when: Apply this to questions about enzymes, digestion, body compartments, or any scenario where location changes conditions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about transport rate, mechanical breakdown, or non-enzymatic processes without evidence that enzyme structure is affected.

Transfer rule: If a mineral can be scratched by a fingernail, then first filter choices by very low hardness before using color or luster.
Error pattern: I overweighted matching appearance and underweighted the decisive hardness constraint from the reference table.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compare the given scratch test to each option’s hardness and eliminate any mineral harder than a fingernail.
Use when: Apply this on mineral-ID questions that provide observable traits plus a hardness clue or scratch-by-common-object test.
Boundary: Ignore this when no hardness evidence is given or when the task depends on another unique property such as streak, acid reaction, or magnetism.

Transfer rule: If an Earth-layer question asks which solid layer moves over a viscous layer, then identify the rigid outer shell above the plastic upper mantle.
Error pattern: Success came from matching physical behavior and relative position, not just picking any named interior layer.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each choice by state and location: rigid solid, viscous/plastic, liquid, or gaseous; then select the solid layer resting atop the viscous one.
Use when: Apply this for geoscience items about mechanical layers, plate motion, or how surface rock interacts with softer material below.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question is about chemical composition, atmospheric zones, or the deepest central region rather than moving surface plates.

Transfer rule: If an impact or friction event produces heat signs like burning odor, warmth, or charring, then classify it as motion/force energy changing into thermal energy.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the observed effect to the resulting energy form instead of being distracted by materials involved.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, list the initial action and the new observable effect; ask whether the effect is heat rather than a substance change.
Use when: Apply this to scenarios with collisions, rubbing, compression, or striking that create temperature-related evidence.
Boundary: Ignore this diagnostic when the main evidence is a new substance, light production, electricity, or motion caused by stored chemical sources.

Transfer rule: If a geology question asks what evidence established a broad crust-movement theory, then prefer measurements that directly track seafloor creation and motion over unrelated rock properties.
Error pattern: Success came from matching the theory to direct, mechanism-level evidence rather than distracting terrestrial or compositional details.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this evidence show new crust forming and a time pattern spreading away from a central source?” If not, reject it.
Use when: The prompt concerns origin of major Earth-science theories, seafloor spreading, crust movement, or evaluating evidence types.
Boundary: Ignore when the question is about local rock identification, weathering, depositional environments, or composition without plate-motion inference.

Transfer rule: If a biology question asks the purpose of mating-season male competition, then prefer the function tied to sexual selection and differential reproductive success.
Error pattern: Success came from identifying the ultimate evolutionary function rather than a nearby procedural or descriptive effect.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask, “Does this option explain how competition changes which individuals leave more offspring?” Reject choices about recognition, communication, or speed alone.
Use when: Apply this on animal behavior items about courtship, contests, mate choice, or traits affecting breeding outcomes across generations.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about immediate mechanisms, species-specific signaling details, or non-evolutionary causes of behavior.

Transfer rule: If asked which trait best aids defense, then choose the feature that directly deters, harms, or warns predators.
Error pattern: Success came from selecting by functional predator-defense value, not by general usefulness or body-shape familiarity.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask “Would this make a predator stop, avoid, or fail to attack right away?” and pick the strongest yes.
Use when: Apply on animal adaptation questions comparing traits with different purposes such as movement, warmth, signaling, or protection.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about another survival function, or when a trait has an indirect ecological role rather than direct defense.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what triggers fight-or-flight, then choose the factor that creates an immediate survival threat or stressor to an individual.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping a biological response to its direct trigger, not to broad background conditions or ecosystem-level goals.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: would this cause instant danger, stress, or resource conflict that demands rapid action by one animal?
Use when: Apply this to biology items about stress responses, behavior, survival mechanisms, or stimulus-to-response matching in animals.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about long-term adaptation, population trends, environmental ethics, or non-immediate ecological effects.

Transfer rule: If asked to identify a carnivore in a food web, then choose the organism that mainly eats other animals, not plants or producers.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying each organism by trophic role before comparing options.
Diagnostic check: For every option, mark producer/herbivore/carnivore/omnivore from its usual diet; commit only if one clearly fits animal-eater.
Use when: This applies to ecology, food web, food chain, predator-prey, or diet-based classification questions.
Boundary: Ignore this when the organism’s diet is explicitly unusual, mixed, life-stage dependent, or the question asks about another role.

Transfer rule: If a switch closes a simple series circuit, then predict the load activates because current can flow.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping circuit state changes to whether the path is complete or broken.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: Is there an unbroken path from source through the device and back? If yes, expect operation.
Use when: Apply this to basic circuit questions about switches, bulbs, and current flow in a single-loop setup.
Boundary: Ignore this when components are faulty, parallel behavior matters, or the question involves voltage, damage, or overheating effects.

Transfer rule: If a trait’s survival benefit is asked, then match the trait to its direct ecological function in that habitat.
Error pattern: Success came from focusing on adaptive camouflage rather than unrelated effects like temperature control, social signaling, or impossible abilities.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this feature reduce detection, improve feeding, aid reproduction, or protect from environment?” and pick the option with the clearest direct mechanism.
Use when: A question links an animal or plant body feature, color, shape, or behavior to survival in a specific setting.
Boundary: Ignore this when the feature is explicitly described as serving communication, physiology, or another non-survival context.

Transfer rule: If a surrounding bath loses ice or warms during a process, then infer the process released heat to the surroundings.  
Error pattern: Success came from tracking energy flow using environmental evidence instead of matching isolated vocabulary.  
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Did the surroundings gain heat or lose heat?” then map gain by surroundings -> release by system; loss by surroundings -> absorption by system.  
Use when: Relevant in thermodynamics questions describing ice melting, temperature change, calorimeters, baths, or other surroundings-based clues.  
Boundary: Ignore this shortcut when melting is caused by external heating, phase changes are unrelated to the reaction, or the system-surroundings boundary is unclear.

Transfer rule: If a question groups elements by table position, then compare broad metallic traits against each choice and prefer the one true for nearly all members.
Error pattern: Success came from using category-level chemistry rather than recalling isolated exceptions or distractor stereotypes.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, mark each option as metallic, nonmetallic, mixed, or unrelated, then reject any trait that conflicts with standard metal behavior.
Use when: This applies to periodic-table region questions asking for a shared physical or chemical property of many elements.
Boundary: Ignore this when the set includes special exceptions, narrow subgroups, or asks about reactivity trends, compounds, or state under nonstandard conditions.

Transfer rule: If a sky event repeats with the lunar phase cycle, then add about one synodic month (~29.5 days) to the observed date and choose the closest matching date.
Error pattern: Replaced a known periodic phenomenon with ad hoc calendar arithmetic instead of using the standard cycle length.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, compute observed date + 29 to 30 days, then verify that earlier choices are far too soon to represent a full repeat.
Use when: The question asks when the Moon will next look the same or be absent/visible again after a given date.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question involves daily rise/set times, location-specific visibility, weather, or non-phase lunar events.

Transfer rule: If choices mix core evolutionary-process traits with guaranteed outcomes or unrelated population claims, then choose the one describing cumulative change across many generations.
Error pattern: Success came from rejecting absolute guarantees and identity requirements while matching the option to the mechanism’s timescale.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, eliminate any choice using words like “guarantees,” requiring all individuals to be the same, or claiming automatic population growth.
Use when: Apply this on biology questions about how adaptation/evolution works, especially definitions of selection versus effects on species or population size.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about short-term ecological change, artificial selection, or a specific population model rather than the general theory.

Transfer rule: If a change reduces prey hiding places without reducing prey presence, then predict higher predator hunting success.
Error pattern: I focused on a downstream hardship for the predator instead of the direct effect of visibility on capture rate.
Diagnostic check: Ask, “Does this environmental change make prey easier or harder to detect or reach right now?” and choose the immediate consequence.
Use when: Food-web questions describe habitat openness, cover removal, camouflage loss, or barriers changing between hunter and prey.
Boundary: Ignore when the change mainly alters predator numbers, prey abundance, migration, weather, or nesting resources rather than encounter/capture conditions.

Transfer rule: If a question asks what a temperature increase means in matter, then map it to greater average particle kinetic motion, not changes in particle size, mass, or count.
Error pattern: Success came from using the particle model and separating thermal effects from structural or identity changes.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Did the particles themselves change, or did only their motion/energy change?” Reject choices altering intrinsic particle properties.
Use when: Apply this to basic heat, temperature, kinetic theory, and states-of-matter questions about what warming does microscopically.
Boundary: Ignore this when the problem involves phase change details, chemical reactions, relativity, or explicitly nonthermal causes.

Transfer rule: If results conflict with a hypothesis after one trial, then repeat the same investigation before changing the idea or method.
Error pattern: Success came from following the scientific-process sequence instead of reacting to unexpected data too quickly.
Diagnostic check: Ask: “Was the procedure already completed once, and am I being tempted to revise the explanation before confirming reliability?”
Use when: A question describes an experiment with surprising results and asks for the immediate next step in the investigation process.
Boundary: Ignore this when repeated trials already exist, the procedure was flawed/unsafe, or the question asks for a later stage like revising explanations.

Transfer rule: If a question asks for the largest object within a named system, then compare all listed bodies by actual physical size, not prominence or planetary status.
Error pattern: Success came from using domain hierarchy correctly and not restricting the search to one subclass such as planets.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, classify each option by body type and ask whether any non-planet category can exceed all planets in size.
Use when: Apply this to astronomy or taxonomy questions mixing categories under one larger system or set.
Boundary: Ignore this when the prompt explicitly limits comparison to a single category or uses a different metric like mass, brightness, or distance.

Transfer rule: If choosing a sample size for more reliable experimental results, then prefer the largest feasible number of trials or subjects offered.
Error pattern: Success came from applying the replication principle: bigger samples reduce random variation and make averages more trustworthy.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, rank the options by sample size and ask, “Would more repeats make the result less dependent on luck?”
Use when: This fits questions about reliability, fairness, consistency, representativeness, or reducing chance effects in experiments or surveys.
Boundary: Ignore this when larger samples add bias, break controls, exceed stated constraints, or when the question asks about cost, speed, or ethics instead.

Transfer rule: If choices mix energy forms, then pick the one involving motion or force doing work on an object.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying examples by energy type instead of surface context or familiar objects.
Diagnostic check: For each option, ask: “Is there observable movement or applied force causing displacement?” Eliminate pure heat, light, or chemical change.
Use when: Apply this to multiple-choice questions asking which example shows mechanical energy, work, or motion-based energy transfer.
Boundary: Ignore this when the target concept is thermal, radiant, electrical, chemical, or when motion is only incidental rather than central.

Transfer rule: If a wave is described as compression/longitudinal, then choose particle displacement parallel to the wave’s travel direction.
Error pattern: I confused longitudinal motion with transverse intuition, reversing the relation between propagation and medium displacement.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Are particles oscillating parallel or perpendicular to the direction the disturbance moves?”
Use when: This applies to questions about wave type, particle motion, sound, slinky compressions, or medium displacement versus propagation.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question concerns transverse waves, field oscillations, or asks about net transport rather than local particle vibration.

Transfer rule: If asked which star is most like the Sun, then first match its evolutionary stage and broad spectral traits before considering anything else.
Error pattern: Success came from classifying stars by lifecycle category instead of being distracted by brightness, fame, or extreme descriptors.
Diagnostic check: For each option, label it as main sequence, giant, dwarf remnant, or supergiant; keep only the one sharing the Sun’s category.
Use when: Apply this on astronomy comparisons involving stellar similarity, especially when choices span very different star classes.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question asks about a different property, such as luminosity, distance, color only, or future evolution.

Transfer rule: If an animal contacts pollen while feeding from flowers, then identify its role as moving pollen between flowers to support plant reproduction.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping a described interaction to a life-cycle function instead of choosing a tempting but unsupported benefit.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: does the passage show transfer of pollen or seeds, and which life-cycle stage does that transfer directly affect?
Use when: Apply this on plant life-cycle questions involving pollinators, nectar feeding, flower visits, or pollen sticking to an animal.
Boundary: Ignore this when the organism’s effect is about defense, nutrient supply, damage, or another process not involving reproductive transfer.

Transfer rule: If a scenario changes only one condition between trials, then infer the investigation targets that changed variable’s effect on the measured outcome.
Error pattern: Success came from isolating the manipulated variable and matching it to the dependent result, not to unrelated goals.
Diagnostic check: List what stays the same and what changes; ask, “What single effect could comparing these trials reveal?”
Use when: Relevant in simple experiment descriptions with repeated actions, one altered condition, and an observed result like distance, time, or speed.
Boundary: Ignore when multiple variables change at once or the question asks for a definition, procedure, or general preference.

Transfer rule: If a device determines distance underwater by sending a pulse and listening for its return, then choose the quantity based on round-trip travel time of the echo.
Error pattern: Success came from mapping the instrument to the standard pulse-echo measurement principle instead of being distracted by wave phenomena that are not directly measured for ranging.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “What observable is compared between emission and return, and can that alone convert to distance using wave speed?”
Use when: Apply this to remote-sensing or navigation questions involving emitted waves, echoes, depth finding, or object-location by pulse methods.
Boundary: Ignore this when the setup emphasizes image formation, medium-bending effects, signal mixing, or direction-finding rather than range measurement.

Transfer rule: If a question asks how to validate reported experimental results, then choose an independent replication of the study under comparable methods.
Error pattern: Success pattern: prioritized external reproducibility over rechecking records, changing methods, or moving to a new question.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, ask: “Which option would most directly show the finding repeats when a separate team performs the test?”
Use when: Apply this to scientific-method items about confirming evidence, reliability, or strengthening confidence in an experimental claim.
Boundary: Ignore this when the task is to generate hypotheses, improve flawed design, analyze data, or identify the next exploratory step.

Transfer rule: If asked where a negatively charged subatomic particle is located in an atom, then place it outside the central core in surrounding regions, not inside it.
Error pattern: Success came from matching charge and typical atomic location instead of being distracted by impossible placements or malformed wording.
Diagnostic check: Before answering, map each listed particle type to charge and usual location; reject any choice that puts the negative one in the core or inside another particle.
Use when: Apply this on basic atomic-structure questions about particle identity, charge, and relative position.
Boundary: Ignore this when the question concerns nonclassical orbitals, exotic states, or asks about behavior rather than location.

Transfer rule: If one organism changes behavior after a stimulus while another is confirmed alive yet shows no change, then infer lack of response to that stimulus, not lack of life or movement.
Error pattern: Correct pattern is isolating the tested variable and rejecting explanations unsupported by the observation.
